entries.helpPage:
# Parse all words

**Parse all words** asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and saves the result against the [Baseline](term:baseline) and the words used for that run.

While it runs, the progress panel stays visible at the top of the window. It shows how many words are done, the word currently being parsed, elapsed time and an estimate of the time left. It also shows the slowest word so far and lists words that stopped at a time or step limit. If no word finishes for a long time, the panel explains that the parser may have stalled and offers **Cancel** and **Report a problem**.

The result tells you which words parsed, which approved analyses PanGloss built again, and how much time parsing took. A search that was interrupted or stopped at a limit is saved as not finished; it should not be read as a completed “no parse.” The **Overview** and **Texts** pages read the saved result. Opening either page does not run PanGloss.

Choose **Parse all words** in the top bar to parse your [Default Selection](term:default-selection) again, or **Refresh** to capture the saved project first. A parse is evidence about one run, not a verdict that the grammar is good or bad.

Motif allows only one Parse all words run for a project at a time, even across windows and processes. If another window is already parsing that project, a second request is refused; use the running window to follow progress or cancel the run.

entries.title: Baseline
entries.description: A Baseline is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the .fwdata file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.
entries.helpPage:
# Baseline

A [Baseline](term:baseline) is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the `.fwdata` file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.

The Baseline is not a backup of linked media, and it is not a live view of FieldWorks. It stays in place until you capture another one. In the window, **Refresh** captures a new Baseline and then measures the current Selection when one is available. Opening the project only reads the Baseline and results already stored.

If the project has changed since the Baseline, Motif can mark its stored numbers as stale. A stale parse and a change that says **No longer fits** are related to different things: one is old measurement evidence; the other is a particular pending choice that no longer matches the project. See [Drift](term:drift).

entries.title: Cancelling a run
entries.description: During Parse all words, choose Cancel in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.
entries.helpPage:
# Cancelling a run

During **Parse all words**, choose **Cancel** in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.

Cancel keeps the results from the previous completed parse. The unfinished parse is not saved, and Motif does not change the FieldWorks project. For other long actions, use the **Cancel** control beside the running action: on **Try a Word**, **AI Handoff**, or beside **Re-run chosen words** in **Timing**. The global progress panel also has **Cancel** while **Refresh** is parsing.

![Parse all words progress and its Cancel control](shot:first-run-setup-parse/cancelling)

entries.title: Changing an analysis
entries.description: In Texts, open the word in Analyze texts, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. For several words at once, the Matrix and Analyze texts can add parser readings as Unknown or mark a spelling Incorrect. The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing an analysis

In **Texts**, open the word in **Analyze texts**, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. For several words at once, the Matrix and **Analyze texts** can add parser readings as Unknown or mark a spelling Incorrect. The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.

The change is kept as pending work for this project. It applies to the word form everywhere, not only the occurrence you were looking at. Look for the count of changes not applied yet, then open **Review changes** to inspect it. Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are choosing or reviewing.

To measure the effect before applying, choose **Check these changes** in Review changes. When you are ready, close FieldWorks and choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. See **Review changes** for the conditions that must be met first.

![A pending choice shown on its word card](shot:explained-word-card/unknown-staged)

entries.title: Default Selection
entries.description: The Default Selection is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each parse keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.
entries.helpPage:
# Default Selection

The [Default Selection](term:default-selection) is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each [parse](term:parse-all-words) keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.

The first time you set up a project, choose texts and add any extra words in **What should Motif measure every time?** Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to edit that choice later. The Selection needs at least one text or added word before Motif can parse.

The Default Selection is not a search query that changes behind your back. Motif resolves the chosen material for each run and records what it measured. Use **Refresh** when you want the saved project and its current Default Selection measured again.

entries.title: Stale numbers and changes
entries.description: In the window, Motif marks a pending change as No longer fits when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.
entries.helpPage:
# Stale numbers and changes

In the window, Motif marks a pending change as [**No longer fits**](term:drift) when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.

For steps to check or remove a change, see **When a change no longer fits**.

entries.title: Choosing what to measure
entries.description: For a new project, choose Refresh after opening it. The first Refresh captures a Baseline and opens setup if no Selection has been saved and setup has not been skipped. Before the first Baseline, Configure… is disabled and its detail reads Refresh first to choose Texts. Setup has four steps: Found the project, choose what to measure, choose parsing limits, and confirm the first run.
entries.helpPage:
# Choosing what to measure

For a new project, choose **Refresh** after opening it. The first Refresh captures a Baseline and opens setup if no Selection has been saved and setup has not been skipped. Before the first Baseline, **Configure…** is disabled and its detail reads **Refresh first to choose Texts**. Setup has four steps: **Found the project**, choose what to measure, choose parsing limits, and confirm the first run.

On **What should Motif measure every time?**, choose one or more texts, or add words in the box labeled **Add words:**. A text’s interlinearized words are what Motif can compare with the analyses already approved in FieldWorks. You can add words that do not occur in the chosen texts. Choose at least one text or add at least one word to continue.

On **How much work should each word get?**, choose a parser step limit. Motif estimates how long a word may take and gives it extra time to finish. The default is 1,000,000 steps. Choose **No step limit** to remove the parser's step limit; with no step limit, Motif applies no time limit.

The last step saves this as the project’s [Default Selection](term:default-selection) and starts the first [parse](term:parse-all-words). Choose **Back** or **Next: texts**, **Next: limits**, and **Next: first run** to move through setup. Choose **Start first run** to save and measure. If you are editing an existing project default, the final action is **Use this Selection**; it saves the choice without starting a run. **Skip for now** closes first-time setup without saving these choices.

On the Texts step and in **Analyze texts**, choose **Select all texts** to check every Text. On a long list, choose **Clear** to uncheck them all. The next parse uses the resulting Selection.

![Choosing texts and added words in first-time setup](shot:first-run-setup-parse/selection)

entries.title: Installing Motif
entries.description: Download the Windows x64 Setup.exe asset from the latest Motif release, run it, and follow the installer. It installs Motif for your Windows user and creates a Start menu shortcut. Launch Motif from that shortcut, then choose Select new… and browse to your FieldWorks .fwdata file.
entries.helpPage:
# Installing Motif

Download the Windows x64 **Setup.exe** asset from the [latest Motif release](https://github.com/sillsdev/motif/releases/latest), run it, and follow the installer. It installs Motif for your Windows user and creates a Start menu shortcut. Launch **Motif** from that shortcut, then choose **Select new…** and browse to your FieldWorks `.fwdata` file.

The official Windows release includes the matching PanGloss parser. You do not need to download PanGloss separately. If you are using a development build instead, parsing requires the `pangloss` executable supplied with that build.

Motif stores project workflow data in a file beside the FieldWorks project: for `Koro.fwdata`, the file is `Koro.motif.db`. It holds Motif’s Baseline, Selection, measurements and pending workflow records; it does not replace the FieldWorks project. When moving or backing up a project, close Motif and copy both files together to the same folder. Open the `.fwdata` file at its new location to continue with the matching Motif data.

entries.title: Affixes, slots, and templates
entries.description: An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A prefix comes before it, a suffix after it, and an infix inside it. As illustrative English examples, un-happy shows a prefix and kind-ness a suffix. The Turkish form evler (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to ev (“house”).
entries.helpPage:
# Affixes, slots, and templates

An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A **prefix** comes before it, a **suffix** after it, and an **infix** inside it. As illustrative English examples, *un-happy* shows a prefix and *kind-ness* a suffix. The Turkish form *evler* (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to *ev* (“house”).

Languages often restrict which affixes can combine and in what order. A **slot** is a position in that sequence. For example, an illustrative verb pattern might allow a person marker before a tense marker. Putting the same affixes in the reverse order could produce a form the language does not use.

In FieldWorks, affix templates organize slots for a part of speech. A noun template can describe noun patterns, while a verb template can describe verb patterns. Some slots are obligatory: a valid word using that template must fill them. Others are optional and may be skipped. These settings help the parser avoid treating every affix as freely combinable with every word.

When a trace reaches the right stem but stops before the expected ending, check the relevant template. Is the affix in the right slot? Is the order right? Is the slot required or optional as intended? Does the template apply to this part of speech? Keep one known word that should use the pattern and one similar word that should not; both help you check whether the template says what you mean.

The examples here are illustrative and simplified. Real languages can have several templates, and a slot can allow more than one affix.

entries.title: Allomorphs and environments
entries.description: One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are allomorphs. The conditions that choose between them are their environments: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.
entries.helpPage:
# Allomorphs and environments

One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are **allomorphs**. The conditions that choose between them are their **environments**: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.

Turkish vowel harmony is a useful real-language example. The plural suffix has the forms *-lar* and *-ler*. In the standard pattern, *-lar* follows a stem with a back last vowel, as in *okullar* (“schools”), and *-ler* follows a stem with a front last vowel, as in *evler* (“houses”). The forms belong to the same plural pattern; the stem’s vowel helps select which one fits.

A **natural class** groups sounds by a shared property, such as “front vowels” or “voiceless consonants.” Instead of writing a separate environment for every vowel, a grammar can use a natural class when the same condition applies to that group. This can make a rule clearer and easier to check.

When the parser builds the stem but cannot use the expected affix form, compare the allomorphs and their environments. Does the needed form exist? Does its environment mention the right sounds or features? Is the environment too narrow, so it misses a valid word, or too broad, so it allows the form where it does not belong?

The Turkish forms illustrate a common pattern; they are not a full account of Turkish. Real patterns may depend on additional features and exceptions.

entries.title: Teach a dumb computer your language
entries.description: You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.
entries.helpPage:
# Teach a dumb computer your language

You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.

The work is a loop:

1. **Measure.** Save your FieldWorks work, then choose **Refresh** or choose [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to measure words you care about. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) tells you how much of the chosen material parsed.
2. **Understand.** Try a difficult word in **Try a Word**. Read the parser’s furthest attempt, then follow its steps to see what it built and where it stopped. Use **Timing** when words take a long time.
3. **Fix.** Use your language knowledge to check the likely cause. Make any grammar or lexicon change in FieldWorks, save it, and measure again.

Motif's synthetic samples are generated to demonstrate its tools and give us small, safe places to practise. They are synthetic-turkic (Turkish-style), synthetic-bantu (Swahili-style), and synthetic-philippine (Tagalog-style), each modelled loosely on the named language. Their data are invented: they are not real language data and must not be used as descriptions of Turkish, Swahili, Tagalog, or any language.

You do not need to become a parser engineer to take part. You can tell an AI consultant what a word should mean and how it is built. Ask it to connect that analysis to the trace, suggest one small change, and name other words that should test the idea. Then check the suggestion against your language knowledge and Motif’s evidence. The AI can help with the machinery; it cannot decide what is right in your language.

entries.title: Modelling grammar in FieldWorks
entries.description: Start with the patterns you want your grammar to describe. Write down what each part means, then compare that account with forms and contrasts in the language.
entries.helpPage:
# Modelling grammar in FieldWorks

Start with the patterns you want your grammar to describe. Write down what each part means, then compare that account with forms and contrasts in the language.

## Start from the language

Write down what each part of your grammar means before you enter it: "the plural is *-ler* after front vowels and *-lar* after back vowels." Use examples from the language to check whether that description fits, including forms that show where the pattern does and does not occur.

## Sounds and spellings

Spelling and sound do not always line up one to one. When a pattern depends on a sound contrast, describe that contrast in the language and consider how the writing system represents it.

## Environments

An environment such as `/ [V] _` describes where an allomorph occurs. Use examples to identify the sounds or features around it, including contexts where a different form occurs.

## Allomorph order

When several allomorphs of one morpheme could fit, the first eligible one wins and blocks the rest. Put the most specific allomorph first and the general one last.

## Slots and templates

An inflectional template describes an order of affix slots. Decide which sequences occur in the language and which positions are optional, then compare the template with forms that illustrate those patterns.

## Features and classes

Features, their values, and inflection classes link by reference, not by name: two things with the same name are not connected. A noun-class system can use both an inflection class and a feature value for each class, as the synthetic Bantu-style sample does, but test agreement on real words before you rely on it.

## When a grammar is slow

When a parse takes longer than expected, use [Timing](cmd:timing) after [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to inspect the recorded run costs before changing the grammar. The Learn page **Why a grammar is slow** explains how to read Timing.

## Change one thing at a time

After each change: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, and check the words you expected to change, plus a few that shouldn't. One change per measurement tells you what each change did.

entries.title: Phonological rules
entries.description: When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonological rules

When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.

English plural endings give an illustrative example of a familiar sound pattern. The ending is usually pronounced with a voiceless [s] after a voiceless sound, as in *cats*, and with [z] after a voiced sound, as in *dogs*. After sibilant sounds, as in *buses*, an extra vowel is heard. These examples show how nearby sounds can affect the way an ending is pronounced; spelling alone does not show every sound detail.

A rule says what changes and in what environment. In plain words, one part of this pattern could be described as “make the ending voiced after a voiced sound.” A well-chosen rule covers the words that share that environment. A rule that is too broad can also change words you meant to leave alone, so check examples from both sides of the pattern.

Rule order matters when one rule changes something that another rule looks for. If Rule 1 creates the sound that Rule 2 needs to see, Rule 1 must apply first. If Rule 2 applies first, it cannot act on a sound that does not exist yet. When a trace shows an unexpected output, check both the rule’s environment and whether earlier rules have already changed the relevant sound.

entries.title: Reading why a word fails
entries.description: Try a Word records the parser's search for one word. Enter it in Type any word..., choose Try it, and read the result. The word can be new; it does not have to occur in the project's texts or lexicon.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading why a word fails

**Try a Word** records the parser's search for one word. Enter it in **Type any word...**, choose **Try it**, and read the result. The word can be new; it does not have to occur in the project's texts or lexicon.

Start with the result and search status:

- **Parsed** means a completed search found an analysis.
- **No parse** with **Search complete** means the search finished without finding an analysis.
- **Search incomplete** means the search did not finish. Read its recorded stop reason; an unfinished search is not evidence that no analysis exists, even when the trace contains no analysis.
- **Nothing to parse** means the grammar's character table does not define a character in the word.

Read any **Analysis summaries** before the **Recorded trace**. Expand tree context to see the recorded events. Select an event to read its exact input, output, raw reason code and captured rejection operands. A rule that was **Tried** was not necessarily **Applied**. **Blocked** names the recorded event without identifying an unrecorded blocker or treating it as the whole word's failure.

**Reason not recorded** and **Rejection details not recorded** mark missing evidence. A raw reason code is separate from the actual features or environment the parser captured. Do not infer a responsible rule from a nearby rejection or assume that every failed path explains the word's result. One attempt may fail while another succeeds.

**Grammar source not recorded** means the page cannot establish the trace's source save. **FieldWorks word context unavailable** means its stored analyses and opinions are unavailable here; it does not mean FieldWorks has no analysis. Use **Analyze texts**, revealed by hover or keyboard focus on the result, to read the word in its text. Use **Full derivation** for the complete recorded tree and filters. The diagnostic tools save the original trace independently of filters.

entries.title: Stems and the lexicon
entries.description: The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.
entries.helpPage:
# Stems and the lexicon

The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.

As an illustrative English example, *walk* is the stem, *to move on foot* is a possible gloss, and *verb* is its part of speech. The form *walked* can be built from that stem and a past-tense ending. A gloss is a short guide for people, not a complete definition or a promise that two languages divide meaning in the same way.

One of the most common causes of failure is a missing stem. If a grammar expects to start with *walk* but that stem is absent or entered under a different form, adding the ending rule will not give the parser a starting point. In a simplified, illustrative Turkish example, the stem *ev* (“house”) is needed before the grammar can analyse *evler* (“houses”) with the plural suffix.

When a word fails, compare the form you typed with the lexicon entry you expect. Check spelling and the relevant writing system, then check that the entry has the stem and part of speech your analysis requires. If the stem is there, move on to the affixes and rules that should build the rest of the word.

The examples here are illustrative; real entries and analyses depend on the language and the choices made in its FieldWorks project.

entries.title: What the parser knows
entries.description: A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current Baseline. It does not know what you meant or guess a missing entry from the conversation.
entries.helpPage:
# What the parser knows

A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current [Baseline](term:baseline). It does not know what you meant or guess a missing entry from the conversation.

A **parse** is an analysis the grammar can build for a word. As an illustrative English example, *cats* can be analysed as the stem *cat* plus the plural ending *-s*. The parser must find a matching stem and a permitted way to combine it with the ending. A word can have more than one possible analysis, and a completed search may find none.

“It doesn’t parse” describes the result for this word and saved grammar. To judge whether that grammar matches the language, compare the result with the forms and patterns speakers use.

First check whether the search completed. A completed search with **No parse** tells you the grammar did not produce a reading. **Search incomplete** means the parser stopped before finishing, so it cannot show that the grammar has no possible analysis. The recorded reason can name a step limit, a time limit or another cause; a missing reason stays unavailable. A word with a character missing from the grammar’s character table is a different case again.

The parser reports what its grammar allowed. You decide whether that grammar matches the language.

entries.title: Why a grammar is slow
entries.description: A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Why a grammar is slow

A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.

An optional slot lets the parser consider a form both with and without that slot. Broad environments let a rule apply in many places, creating more possible continuations. An empty affix adds no visible letters, so the parser can add it without consuming part of the word, though PanGloss often handles these cheaply: in the synthetic Bantu-style sample, 160 empty allomorphs added no measurable work. A duplicated real affix is different; there, copying one object marker into a second slot multiplied the work.

Use [Timing](cmd:timing) after [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to locate recorded parse time. **Timing** groups time first by kind of rule, then by rule, and then shows slow words. Start with **Slowest** or **All**, select a costly rule, and look at the words that use it. Timing reports where time was spent; it does not record what caused the work. Compare the words and grammar around a costly rule, then choose what to inspect.

Check that each optional slot is truly optional, each environment names the sounds it should, and each affix appears only once. Change one thing at a time and measure again. If a search stopped at the step limit, raise **Step limit** under **Re-run**; if it ran out of time, increase **Seconds per word** there. A timing result shows where work was spent, while your language knowledge helps decide whether the grammar can be made more specific.

entries.title: Working with an AI consultant
entries.description: You bring knowledge of the language. An AI consultant can help connect that knowledge to parser rules and FieldWorks settings. Motif adds evidence: AI Handoff writes a folder you can choose to share with a chat model. It contains selected project material and, when available, the results of Parse all words with a starter question. The folder can contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences, so read the notice and share it only with a service you trust.
entries.helpPage:
# Working with an AI consultant

You bring knowledge of the language. An AI consultant can help connect that knowledge to parser rules and FieldWorks settings. Motif adds evidence: **AI Handoff** writes a folder you can choose to share with a chat model. It contains selected project material and, when available, the results of [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) with a starter question. The folder can contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences, so read the notice and share it only with a service you trust.

Ask a focused question. For example: “This word should be stem plus plural. The trace stops at this affix. Which slot or environment would you check first? What evidence supports that, and what other words would distinguish your suggestion from an alternative?” Ask for one small proposed change and examples that should still fail. You can ask the AI to explain parser terminology, but check every claim about your language against what speakers say and use.

Treat the answer as a hypothesis, not an instruction. Check that it accounts for the failing word without breaking a known-good word. If you decide to change the grammar or lexicon, make the edit in FieldWorks, save, then choose **Refresh** and inspect the new evidence in Motif.

**Review changes** has a narrower role: it reviews pending analysis choices made in Motif. If the AI suggests choosing or changing an analysis for a word, make that choice through **Texts**, then open **Review changes**. Inspect the word and action, choose **Check these changes** to measure their effect, and apply only if the changes still fit and the evidence is current. Review changes does not import an AI answer or apply grammar edits; your judgement remains in charge.

entries.title: Opening a project
entries.description: Open the project menu and choose Select new… to browse for a FieldWorks .fwdata file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose Open recent and select it. The window opens on Overview and reads the project’s stored Baseline, Selection, and results; opening it does not automatically take a new measurement.
entries.helpPage:
# Opening a project

Open the project menu and choose **Select new…** to browse for a FieldWorks `.fwdata` file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose **Open recent** and select it. The window opens on **Overview** and reads the project’s stored Baseline, Selection, and results; opening it does not automatically take a new measurement.

If this project has no Baseline yet, press **Refresh**. Motif reads the saved `.fwdata` file to capture the Baseline. Save your latest edits in FieldWorks first if you want them included: unsaved edits in FieldWorks are not part of the file Motif reads. You do not have to close FieldWorks just to open a project, though a capture may be refused while another program holds the project.

For a project without a saved Default Selection, setup opens once a Baseline is available, unless setup was skipped. On a new project, the first **Refresh** captures the Baseline and opens setup. Before that first Baseline, **Configure…** is disabled and its detail reads **Refresh first to choose Texts**. In setup, choose texts or add words, set the parsing limits, and start the first run. You can choose **Skip for now** and use **Configure…** later to reopen setup.

FieldWorks must be closed before you apply changes from Motif. This is separate from opening the project or reading its last saved state.

![A project open on the Overview](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: Overview
entries.description: Overview is the first page when you open a project. It gathers stored results and project counts so you can see where things stand without starting a new run.
entries.helpPage:
# Overview

**Overview** is the first page when you open a project. It gathers stored results and project counts so you can see where things stand without starting a new run.

Use **Look first** to open the saved words or timings behind a measured group. A word can hold Unknown and Disapproved analyses at the same time; its Matrix row summarizes what FieldWorks holds, while each analysis keeps its own opinion. When PanGloss matched an analysis FieldWorks marked Disapproved, the word can appear in **Unknown × Different**; its row uses the cell's **Differs: have a look** meaning and shows recorded comparison detail beneath it. Compare the analyses before deciding what opinion to record. A stopped search does not establish which analyses were not built.

The top card shows the project and its counts: words in the Selection, places, wordforms, rules, and lexemes. Four cards follow. **Speed** shows how many words PanGloss timed, their total word time (each word's parse time added up), the median time for a word, and a compact line of the slowest words and their recorded times. A word stopped at the step limit is marked **Stopped**. **Text coverage** shows how many of the words in your Selection parse, and how many of their places. **Approved analyses kept** shows how many of the words you approved in FieldWorks the grammar still builds. **Grammar warnings** shows the warning, error, and information finding counts from a grammar check, including how many findings are errors. These are separate measures, not one overall score.

The slowest words include searches that stopped. Project wordforms, rules and lexemes come from the Baseline and remain available before parsing; parse measurements stay absent until a run is recorded. The warnings count is the same count shown beside Warnings.

The top bar says whether these numbers are current. If FieldWorks has saved since they were measured, the freshness line gives the save time and Baseline time once. Press **Refresh** when you are ready to capture the saved project and measure the [Default Selection](term:default-selection) again. If Motif cannot read the numbers, the page says so in one line, with **Try again** and **Report a problem**.

Choose a card's link, such as **Slowest words →**, **Texts →**, **Matrix →**, or **Warnings →**, to see more on that page. Hover over or focus a card to show its link. Each **Look first** row opens the words or timings it names; hover or focus the row to show its word-count link. Expand **Project history** to see recorded activity. For a closer explanation of each measure and how to read its breakdowns, see [Reading the Overview](guide:reading-the-overview).

![Overview showing the project's stored results](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: PanGloss
entries.description: On Analyze texts, PanGloss runs the project's grammar on selected texts and compares its readings with what FieldWorks stores.
entries.helpPage:
# PanGloss

On Analyze texts, PanGloss runs the project's grammar on selected texts and compares its readings with what FieldWorks stores.

PanGloss parses XAmple and HermitCrab grammars fast. Fully compatible.

A means Approved, U means Unknown, D means Disapproved, and a dashed mark means FieldWorks has no reading stored. Blue means PanGloss found a new or different reading. Staged means a choice is waiting for Apply to FieldWorks project.

![The compact word strip for geldi](shot:explained-word-card/approved-agrees)

entries.title: Pending changes
entries.description: Pending changes are the analysis choices you have collected in Motif but have not yet written to FieldWorks. They can come from Texts and are listed together on Review changes. The window labels them as “changes not applied yet.”
entries.helpPage:
# Pending changes

Pending changes are the analysis choices you have collected in Motif but have not yet written to FieldWorks. They can come from **Texts** and are listed together on **Review changes**. The window labels them as “changes not applied yet.”

Use **Undo** on **Review changes** to withdraw a choice, or return to **Texts** to make a different choice for the same word and analysis. The list belongs to its project and remains available if you close Motif and open that project again.

Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are collecting or reading these changes. Before applying, use **Check these changes** to measure the touched words, confirm that the evidence is current and complete, and make sure every choice still fits. Then choose **Apply to FieldWorks project** while FieldWorks is closed.

This page describes the window’s “changes not applied yet” wording. The related stored-change concept is linked here as [pending changes](term:proposal).

entries.title: Reading the Overview
entries.description: The Overview brings together saved results and project counts. Its cards answer different questions: how long words took to parse, how many words in your Selection parse, how many Approved analyses the grammar still builds, and what the grammar check found. Read each card's labels and breakdowns separately; the headline numbers are not one combined score.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading the Overview

The [Overview](term:overview) brings together saved results and project counts. Its cards answer different questions: how long words took to parse, how many words in your Selection parse, how many Approved analyses the grammar still builds, and what the grammar check found. Read each card's labels and breakdowns separately; the headline numbers are not one combined score.

For the full page tour—including freshness, Text Coverage, timing, warnings and the links behind each card—see [Overview](guide:overview). Opening the page shows stored results; it does not start a parse. To measure the current [Default Selection](term:default-selection) against the saved FieldWorks project, choose **Refresh** or **Parse all words** as described in [Parse all words](guide:assessment).

entries.title: Refreshing numbers
entries.description: Use Refresh after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif’s results to reflect that saved state. Refresh is an action, not an automatic update: it captures a new Baseline from the saved project, checks the grammar for Warnings, and parses the words in the current Default Selection, when one is available.
entries.helpPage:
# Refreshing numbers

Use **Refresh** after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif’s results to reflect that saved state. Refresh is an action, not an automatic update: it captures a new [Baseline](term:baseline) from the saved project, checks the grammar for **Warnings**, and parses the words in the current [Default Selection](term:default-selection), when one is available.

1. Save your work in FieldWorks.
2. In Motif, choose **Refresh** in the top bar and let it finish.
3. Check the freshness line and the updated cards on **Overview**. The new [parse](term:parse-all-words) saves what was measured.

If this is the first Baseline, first-time setup may open so you can choose texts or add words before the first parse. If you cancel the run or the parser refuses it, the Baseline may still be newer than the numbers; read the freshness message before relying on them. Opening Motif again does not perform a Refresh for you.

![Refresh captures a Baseline before a separate parse updates the numbers](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/refreshed)

entries.title: Changing a pending change
entries.description: You can change your mind before Apply. To replace a pending opinion, return to Texts, open the same word form, choose the reading or action you want instead, and collect that change. A new choice for the same word and analysis slot replaces the earlier pending choice.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing a pending change

You can change your mind before Apply. To replace a pending opinion, return to **Texts**, open the same word form, choose the reading or action you want instead, and collect that change. A new choice for the same word and analysis slot replaces the earlier pending choice.

To remove a change without replacing it:

1. Open **Review changes**.
2. Find the word and action you want to withdraw.
3. Choose **Undo** beside it.

The remaining pending changes stay in the list. Use **Keep editing** to return to the page where the first pending change was collected. Changes belong to the project and remain available if you close Motif and open that project again.

![A staged choice before you replace or undo it](shot:explained-word-card/unknown-staged)

entries.title: Review changes
entries.description: Review changes gathers the analysis changes you have collected from other pages, grouped by what they do. For each word, it shows its analysis, the staged change, and whether the change still fits the current FieldWorks project. Reading this page does not apply anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Review changes

**Review changes** gathers the analysis changes you have collected from other pages, grouped by what they do. For each word, it shows its analysis, the staged change, and whether the change still fits the current FieldWorks project. Reading this page does not apply anything.

1. Check each listed word and change. Choose **Undo** beside a change you no longer want, or **Undo all** to take back a whole group.
2. Choose **Check these changes** to measure the words you touched and see **What applying does to the numbers**. If the check is still running, you can choose **Cancel**.
3. Read what blocks Apply. The page title counts the changes that block Apply; the Apply card lists the reasons and the action that clears each one. Apply only when the changes still fit, the numbers are current, the evidence is complete, FieldWorks is not holding the project open, and no approved analysis would be lost.
4. Choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. After a successful Apply, the page shows a receipt. There is no extra confirmation step.

If a change says **No longer fits**, Apply stays blocked. Remove that change or refresh the project and check it again. A change that no longer fits cannot be forced. See **When a change no longer fits** for steps to recheck it.

If a change is **Uncertain**, its sentence changed in FieldWorks after you made it. The page shows the sentence as it reads now. Choose **Check again** to keep the change, or **Undo** to take it back.

If Motif could not confirm an Apply, the page says that FieldWorks may already have these changes. Choose **Refresh** to check what the project holds now. Apply stays blocked until you do.

![Review changes after measuring a pending analysis change](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/measured)

entries.title: Switching projects
entries.description: Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.
entries.helpPage:
# Switching projects

Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.

1. Choose **Select new…** to browse for a `.fwdata` file, or choose **Open recent** and select a project Motif already knows.
2. Wait for the project’s Baseline, Selection, and stored results to load.
3. Check the project name on **Overview** before taking an action.

Each project has its own Motif workflow information. Switching away does not move its pending changes into another project; when you open it again, its changes are shown with that project. If Parse all words or AI Handoff is running, switching projects cancels that work before Motif loads the new project.

Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to reopen the project’s saved Selection and parsing limits. Use **Refresh** when you want a new Baseline and measurement; opening the project alone only reads stored results.

![The Overview after selecting a project](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: Text Coverage
entries.description: Text Coverage shows what share of the Default Selection’s words, and their places in the chosen Texts, parsed in the last saved parse. The Overview reports both selected words and their places, so the two numbers may differ: one word form can appear many times in a Text.
entries.helpPage:
# Text Coverage

[Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) shows what share of the Default Selection’s words, and their places in the chosen Texts, parsed in the last saved parse. The Overview reports both selected words and their places, so the two numbers may differ: one word form can appear many times in a Text.

Use the breakdown to see parsed words alongside words with no parse, incomplete searches, or other recorded outcomes. A word that reached a time or step limit did not complete its search, so read that outcome separately from a completed search with no parse.

Text Coverage is about the selected Texts and words. It is not the same as **Accuracy**, which compares parser readings with approved analyses, or grammar coverage over an outside Corpus. Choose **Texts** to inspect words and places; read [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to understand which run the Overview is showing.

entries.title: Texts
entries.description: Texts is where you choose material to measure and compare word analyses. Its tabs are Matrix, Analyze texts, Lists, and What changed. In Analyze texts, use Read text to follow words in context or Word list to inspect words directly. Choose texts or added words there, then use Parse all words to record results for that Selection. When the Inspector is open, the text-selection list folds away so the text picker stays in view.
entries.helpPage:
# Texts

**Texts** is where you choose material to measure and compare word analyses. Its tabs are **Matrix**, **Analyze texts**, **Lists**, and **What changed**. In **Analyze texts**, use **Read text** to follow words in context or **Word list** to inspect words directly. Choose texts or added words there, then use **Parse all words** to record results for that Selection. When the Inspector is open, the text-selection list folds away so the text picker stays in view.

The Matrix groups words by what FieldWorks holds, down the side, and what PanGloss found, across the top: **Same**, **Different**, **No parse**, **Stopped** or **Not parsed**. Each cell says in a few words what happened, such as **Kept**, **Lost** or **Built anyway**. It names both counts when words and places differ (for example, **4 words · 7 places**), and says **1 place** when the counts are the same. Point at a cell to read what its words have in common. The chips above the Matrix, such as **Lost** or **New: PanGloss proposes**, choose those cells for you.

Every word row uses the meaning named by its Matrix cell, including in **Lists** and **Analyze texts**. A card may show recorded comparison detail beneath that shared meaning. For example, a word with Unknown and Disapproved analyses can appear in **Unknown × Different** when PanGloss matched an analysis FieldWorks marked Disapproved; the row keeps the cell's **Differs: have a look** meaning and shows recorded comparison detail beneath it. When Approved and Disapproved analyses share a morphology, both opinions remain visible; that match does not establish which other analyses PanGloss matched.

An **Analyze texts** card can also show which FieldWorks item a grammar warning names in that word. **Other words that use -a** lists words with the same named item. Membership and spelling matches stay labelled as possible matches. This evidence records a connection to the warning; it does not say the warning caused the word's result. Open the warning to read PanGloss's full description.

A stopped search does not establish that an analysis was not built, even if it found some readings. Those words stay in **Stopped**, with **No result**; a word that was not parsed has no new comparison evidence. Matrix, the shared word lists and **Analyze texts** use the same per-word comparison.

**Word list** counts words by their FieldWorks opinion, with a separate filter for Approved, Unknown, Disapproved and Not in FieldWorks. These counts describe words, while each analysis in a word card keeps its own opinion. The shared row also shows the meaning, places and time. Identical forms and glosses can still name different morphemes; the list explains that identity difference beside the readings instead of treating spelling as a match.

Select a cell to list its words below the Matrix. The list's heading names the cell and says in one line what it means. When two or more of its words use the same morpheme, **What these words share** shows each such morpheme and how many of the words use it. Morphemes are matched by their identity in FieldWorks, never by spelling, and a shared one is often the first clue to a single cause. Choose a morpheme to open it in the Inspector; its FieldWorks link appears when you point at or focus it. Choose **Open in text** to see a word in **Analyze texts**. For ticked words, the Matrix offers **Add as Unknown** and **Incorrect spelling**. Approving, disapproving or making an analysis Unknown happens one analysis at a time, in **Analyze texts**. Each action applies to the word form everywhere in the project, not only the occurrence currently shown.

**Lists** holds the Matrix's named shortcuts, such as **Lost** or **Built something else**, with the same words, and opens on the first list that has words. One line names the list, counts its words and places, and says what it holds. Open a word to see the same FieldWorks and PanGloss card used in the Matrix; its morphemes open in the Inspector, and FieldWorks links appear when you point at or focus a morpheme. Tick words to send just those: the button says **AI Handoff for this word** or names the number of words. **AI Handoff for this list** sends every word in the selected list. With no words ticked, **AI Handoff** is disabled and explains **Tick words first.** A list of stopped or unparsed words also offers **Parse again**. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text, never from a list.

Changes you collect remain pending until you review and apply them. The page’s **Review changes** link opens that list; it does not write anything to FieldWorks. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) appears on the Overview after a measurement.

![Texts after Parse all words records the current comparison](shot:open-project-overview/texts)

entries.title: Timing
entries.description: Timing opens on All and shows recorded parse times for the current Selection. It reads timing saved by Parse all words; opening the page does not start a parse. If there is no timing for those words, choose Parse again. If Step limit or Slowest has no words, choose Show all words to return to the full Selection.
entries.helpPage:
# Timing

**Timing** opens on **All** and shows recorded parse times for the current Selection. It reads timing saved by [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words); opening the page does not start a parse. If there is no timing for those words, choose **Parse again**. If **Step limit** or **Slowest** has no words, choose **Show all words** to return to the full Selection.

The **Words** row shows **All**, **Stopped**, and **Slowest** with their word counts. Choose **A Matrix cell** or **A list** to pick words from Texts; open **More** for words checked in Texts or words you enter by hand. **AI Handoff for these words** uses the current word group. **Re-run** opens the per-word time and step limits and the run controls. Its step limit starts at 1,000,000. Shares use whole percentages; a positive share below one percent says **<1%**. **Not attributed** appears once in the kind legend for time the parser did not assign to a rule or lookup. **Overrun** is object time measured beyond total word time, shown separately without an assumed cause. Open **Show calls** to see each kind's recorded call count; a kind that does not count calls says **Not counted**.

The compact word row names PanGloss's outcome as **Same**, **Different**, **No parse**, or **Stopped**. The meaning is separate and hidden in this list; a matching morphology alone does not imply agreement with a Disapproved opinion.

Select a rule row to see its costliest words; open **Inspect** on the row to see its FieldWorks facts and link. While the Inspector is open, the rule table uses the available width and hides **Kind**. An amber warning mark means the stored rule identity is structural, synthetic, or unavailable. The inspector separates words that use a morpheme in a stored analysis from words where the parser tried it. Its word and call counts come from that item’s recorded timers; if none were recorded, it says so. In **Detailed statistics**, word time keeps one shading scale across the selected words. **By word** uses those same words; other groups show the complete parse and say so.

The **Slowest** list includes stopped searches when they have a recorded time; each stopped word says whether it reached the step or time limit. To measure selected words again, open **Re-run**, choose **Seconds per word** or **Step limit**, then choose **Re-run chosen words**. The step limit starts at **1,000,000**. **Cancel** stops that rerun. When you retry, raise **Step limit** after a step-limit stop or increase **Seconds per word** after a time-limit stop. When the current totals include re-runs, Timing labels the number of separate measurements. The Detailed statistics card says whether its slowest measured word finished or stopped; when completion is unavailable, it says **Slowest measured word**. Open **Detailed statistics** to load its rows; changing the group loads the new group.

The **Readings** count in Detailed statistics reports how many words produced more than one reading. That count does not tell you why. It may reflect different words with the same spelling or several analyses the grammar allows; inspect the words' readings to tell them apart. A rule's time share says how much time its timer recorded, not what caused a word to parse or stop.

![Saved parse timings on the Timing page](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/timing)

entries.title: Try a Word
entries.description: Use Try a Word to trace one word through the grammar. The word does not need to appear in a chosen text or exist in the FieldWorks project.
entries.helpPage:
# Try a Word

Use **Try a Word** to trace one word through the grammar. The word does not need to appear in a chosen text or exist in the FieldWorks project.

1. Enter a word in **Type any word...**.
2. Choose **Try it** and wait for the trace. Choose **Cancel** to interrupt a running search.
3. Read the result and any search limit. **Search incomplete** takes precedence even if the parser found an analysis; an unfinished search cannot establish that no analysis exists.
4. Read the result summary and analysis cards, then **Recorded trace**. Each summary groups analyses with proven equal morphology. **Recorded twice** counts source records; it does not establish two different derivations. Unprojected parser morpheme names remain available in **Parser record** in **Expert**.
5. Select a recorded event to read its explanation. Plain uses a known explanation when one is available; otherwise it says **PanGloss didn't record why.**

Choose **Plain** or **Expert** beside **Try it**. The filled control shows the selected view. The installed window remembers your choice. Switching keeps the same recorded attempt, selected event address and open inspector; it does not run the parser again. Addresses identify occurrences within this saved trace, not across newly generated traces.

**Plain** shows compact recorded steps with their forms before and after. Rule levels and lexical lookups are counted in a folded line and remain available in **Expert**. Select a step to read its sentence directly beneath that row. A refused step differs from a search stopped at its limit: **No analysis found** means that a recorded attempt failed. The rows preserve the recorded order and do not infer a cause from neighboring events.

**Expert** keeps event names, subrule indices and input/output shapes in the parser's order, including both recorded passes. Missing input and output values appear blank; focus their tokens to learn that they were not recorded. A subrule appears only when the parser recorded a positive index. Choose **Show one analysis path** and turn off **Every step** to read its recorded ancestors and terminal event. **Showing every step** includes other search context; neighboring events alone never establish attempt membership or a cause. **Phonological rules applied** lists recorded phonological events in the chosen view, with each event's own outcome. **Tried** does not mean **Applied**, and an unchanged shape does not prove application. **Parser record** starts folded and keeps the exact source analyses, producer identifiers, projection details and unprojected morpheme names. FieldWorks morpheme forms appear only when their projections are available; parser names alone do not establish a FieldWorks analysis.

Select an event to read its sentence directly beneath the event row. The selected event's **Parser record** and rejection details start folded. The record preserves unknown producer fields and omits its children from this detail view; saving still keeps the whole diagnostic. Tokens explain themselves on hover or keyboard focus. **Environment notation** keeps the recorded diagnostic operand intact and shows **Authored environment notation unavailable**. Decoding requires the trace to explicitly identify authored environment text; the supported trace formats do not establish it. Strings, structured operands and punctuation such as `/`, `_`, `#`, brackets, parentheses and `?` cannot establish that language by themselves, so they remain raw.

**Reason not recorded**, **Rejection details not recorded**, **The grammar of this trace was not recorded**, and **FieldWorks word context unavailable** identify facts the page cannot establish. Missing word context does not mean the word is absent from FieldWorks. The recorded tree shows search context; neighboring events alone do not establish which rule caused an attempt to fail.

**FieldWorks beside the parser** shows every stored analysis for the returned word, whether the trace parsed it or not, with **Approved**, **Disapproved** or **Unknown** beside each analysis. The result line also names the recorded opinions. A completed search that finds no analysis shows the same meaning as the Matrix, such as **Lost** for an Approved word. An unfinished search cannot establish that an Approved analysis was lost. Save and Baseline times use the computer's local time. **FieldWorks saved since** appears only when the recorded save time is later than the Baseline capture. A word absent from that Baseline differs from a wordform with no stored analyses. Unknown membership and unavailable context remain explicit.

**No terminal attempt was recorded before the search stopped** marks an interrupted search without a terminal attempt. Its recorded progress remains available in the tree. Recorded terminal attempts show only their returned reasons and attribution. **Steps on this path** lists actual ancestors and the terminal event; **Recorded tree context** shows nearby events whose membership is not established. Event addresses identify repeated occurrences within this saved trace, and the small notation names the recorded pass and outcome.

An earlier parse's measured times appear in a separate block named by the word's recorded measurement time. The block stays hidden when that source time was not recorded. They cover that parse's whole search for the word, including stopped attempts. They are not times for a step in this trace. Shares use that measurement's word time; **Not attributed** and any timer overrun appear only when the measurement recorded them.

Hover over the result or use keyboard focus to reveal **Analyze texts**, **Timing**, and **AI Handoff**. **Analyze texts** opens the returned word in its text, where opinions are changed. These actions keep addressing the displayed result when you edit or clear the input for another Try. **AI Handoff** keeps this diagnostic and the Baseline recorded with it; it does not parse the word again or make a replacement trace. The menu beside **Try it** contains recent words and tools for copying, saving or opening a trace. **Copy for a chat model** includes the instructions, one-line summary, and original diagnostic JSON. **Full derivation** starts folded and provides all recorded steps and filters. Saving keeps the original diagnostic regardless of display filters.

Both views name the Baseline that actually produced the trace, using its capture time in the computer's local time. A trace without a recorded Baseline says so. When the earlier parse and the trace record different Baseline identities, the page says **This trace and the earlier parse used different Baselines. Refresh and try again.** That difference does not establish that a grammar change caused a failed search. Capture details keep the source project's save time as well. A Refresh published while a request waits can change which Baseline it uses. An older workspace description cannot relabel the returned evidence.

Recorded details can include the replacement lexical entry for a Blocked event, the template slots a branch applied or skipped, and the completion gate that ended a partial attempt. A completed lookup records how many possible roots it returned; those are not counts of successful analyses. Typed rejection details retain the operands PanGloss actually tested, including any authored environment identity and text. A phonological step with an unavailable reason remains unknown.

A Blocked event records an intermediate result. In the supported parser it means replacement by a compatible entry in the same lexical family; search can continue. Missing reasons, rejection details and grammar sources are shown as not recorded, and unfamiliar reason codes keep their raw notation with an unavailable explanation.


![A word parsed in Try a Word](shot:try-word-typing/trace)

The main analysis cards combine source records only when available projections establish equal ordered allomorph and grammatical information identities, including inflection type. Equal spellings alone do not establish that they are the same analysis. The recorded source list keeps every producer record.

entries.title: Warnings
entries.description: Warnings shows findings from a check of the whole grammar. They are stored for the Baseline, and do not depend on which texts or words you selected. PanGloss may include an explanation or guidance with each finding.
entries.helpPage:
# Warnings

**Warnings** shows findings from a check of the whole grammar. They are stored for the [Baseline](term:baseline), and do not depend on which texts or words you selected. PanGloss may include an explanation or guidance with each finding.

If the grammar has not been checked for this Baseline, choose **Check the grammar again**. PanGloss reads the whole grammar, so a check can take a minute for a large project. **Refresh** captures a new Baseline and checks the grammar again. Later visits show the stored findings; opening the page does not start a check.

The filter chips count findings by report level. Identical findings with no named item share one row, with the repeated count beside the title. **Touch your words** shows the number of distinct Selection words matched to named FieldWorks items, when that count is available. Turn it on to show only findings with those matches. The **Sort** menu orders the rows by that same count or by the order in the report.

A finding may have exact word uses, words reached only by membership or spelling, or no word list. Membership and spelling remain labelled because neither confirms an exact use of the named item. **None of your words** means PanGloss named an item but no Selection word matched it. When a word count cannot be established, Motif leaves it unavailable instead of showing zero. If PanGloss names no item, the row says so.

Open a row to read PanGloss's full description and any explanation or guidance it supplied. **What to do in FieldWorks** appears only when PanGloss supplied guidance. The named item opens in FieldWorks only when PanGloss supplied a verified destination. If a finding no longer appears after **Refresh**, its row says **Gone after Refresh**. Save edits in FieldWorks, refresh Motif, then parse the affected words again to see their current results.

![Grammar findings saved for the current Baseline](shot:warnings-filter/findings)

PanGloss supplies each finding's title, description, explanation and guidance in the report's recorded language. **Learn more** opens its reference when available. Motif displays that text without adding advice of its own.

A missing or unresolved subject has no object link. A project setting has no individual object to open. A named live object opens only through the destination PanGloss supplied; Motif does not infer a destination from the finding's sentence.

entries.title: What Motif does
entries.description: Motif helps you measure how a FieldWorks grammar works, inspect individual words, and collect changes to word analyses before applying them. It reads the saved FieldWorks project; FieldWorks remains the place where the project’s linguistic data lives.
entries.helpPage:
# What Motif does

Motif helps you measure how a FieldWorks grammar works, inspect individual words, and collect changes to word analyses before applying them. It reads the saved FieldWorks project; FieldWorks remains the place where the project’s linguistic data lives.

Motif uses PanGloss to parse words. [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) saves what a run measured. The [Overview](term:overview) shows stored results such as Text Coverage, accuracy against approved analyses, timing, and grammar warnings. It does not start a new run just because you open the window. Start with [Opening a project](guide:open-a-project) to capture the saved project and choose words to measure.

When you want current numbers, press **Refresh**. Motif captures a [Baseline](term:baseline) from the saved project and measures the project’s [Default Selection](term:default-selection). In **Texts**, you can inspect words and choose analysis changes. **Review changes** lets you check those changes and see whether they still fit before you choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. The guides for [Refresh](guide:refresh-numbers), [Texts](guide:texts) and [Review changes](guide:review-changes) explain those steps.

You can also make an **AI Handoff** folder with project context and a question for a chat model. Review the data-sensitivity notice before sharing it: the folder can contain real grammar, lexicon, and text data.

![Motif’s Overview after opening a project](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: When a change no longer fits
entries.description: When a pending change is marked No longer fits, use these steps to check the original choice against the current project.
entries.helpPage:
# When a change no longer fits

When a pending change is marked **No longer fits**, use these steps to check the original choice against the current project.

1. Open **Review changes**. Changes that no longer fit are in the **No longer fits** group at the top of the page, and each one says what changed in FieldWorks.
2. If you want to keep trying the change, save the project in FieldWorks, then choose **Refresh** in Motif.
3. In the **No longer fits** group, choose **Check again**. Motif checks whether the original identities still fit.
4. If it still says **No longer fits**, choose **Remove the ones that no longer fit**, or choose **Undo** beside one change. Return to **Texts** and make a new choice against the current project.

Apply remains blocked while any change no longer fits. The window does not offer a way to force a change that no longer fits.

![Review changes with a choice marked No longer fits](shot:no-longer-fits/review)

entries.title: When something goes wrong
entries.description: If a command or action is refused, first read the message in Motif. It often explains what needs to change, such as saving in FieldWorks, refreshing the Baseline, or removing a change that no longer fits.
entries.helpPage:
# When something goes wrong

If a command or action is refused, first read the message in Motif. It often explains what needs to change, such as saving in FieldWorks, refreshing the Baseline, or removing a change that no longer fits.

For a parser trace, open **Diagnostic tools** from **Try a Word**. You can save or copy diagnostic information for a particular word. It can include real word forms and morphological details, so review it before sharing.

If the app stops after an error, the separate **Motif has stopped** window offers **Copy details**, **Save report**, **Email maintainer**, and **Close**. Include what you were doing, the page, the error message, and steps that reproduce it. Check any saved report or diagnostic for project or linguistic information before sending it to someone else.
